citations.quote:
For Burgers' flux $f_B(s)=s^2/2$, define $G\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ as follows. If $a\le b$, set
$$ G(a,b)=\begin{cases} a^2/2,&a\ge0,\\ b^2/2,&a<0\text{ and }b\le0,\\ 0,&a<0<b. \end{cases} $$ If $b<a$, set $$ G(a,b)=\frac12\max\{a^2,b^2\}. $$
This is the Godunov flux for the convex Burgers flux: for increasing states it
uses the minimum of $f_B$ on $[a,b]$, and for decreasing states it uses the
maximum of $f_B$ on $[b,a]$. It is proposed as a particular numerical flux in
the scheme of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Its continuity and
consistency are verified in the pair.

derivations.claim: On each open region cut out by $a=b$, $a=0$, and $b=0$, the displayed formula in [F1] is either a polynomial, zero, or $(a^2+b^2+|a^2-b^2|)/4$, so it is continuous there.

At a boundary with $a=b>0$ both adjacent formulas tend to $a^2/2$; at $a=b<0$ both tend to $a^2/2$; at $a=0\le b$ the left and right limits are zero; at $a\le0=b$ the limits are zero. On the remaining axis portions $a=0>b$ and $b=0<a$, a neighborhood lies in the single shock branch $b<a$, whose formula is continuous there. At $(a,b)=(0,0)$ every branch has absolute value at most $\max\{a^2,b^2\}/2$, which tends to zero. These checks cover every branch boundary and prove continuity on all of $\mathbb R^2$.
On the diagonal, if $a\ge0$ the first branch gives $G(a,a)=a^2/2$; if $a<0$ the second branch gives $G(a,a)=a^2/2$. Thus $G(a,a)=f_B(a)$ for all $a$, and [F2] makes $G$ a consistent numerical flux.

derivations.claim: Multiply [F1] by $\Phi_j^{m,n}$ and sum over $j\in\mathbb Z$ and $n=0,\ldots,N-1$. Only finitely many terms are nonzero, so the summed update is an exact finite sum equal to zero.

For each fixed $j$, telescoping gives $$ \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(U_j^{m,n+1}-U_j^{m,n})\Phi_j^{m,n} =-U_j^{m,0}\Phi_j^{m,0} +\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}U_j^{m,n}(\Phi_j^{m,n-1}-\Phi_j^{m,n}), $$ since $\Phi_j^{m,N-1}=0$ by the terminal support condition.

Reindex the spatial flux sum: $$ \sum_j(Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n}-Q_{j-1/2}^{m,n})\Phi_j^{m,n} =\sum_jQ_{j+1/2}^{m,n}(\Phi_j^{m,n}-\Phi_{j+1}^{m,n}). $$ Substitute this and step 2.1 into step 1.1, then multiply the zero identity by $-1$ to obtain exactly the displayed formula.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the cells, time levels, states and interface fluxes from
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. For $J_n^m=[t_n^m,t_{n+1}^m)$,
the **piecewise-constant state reconstruction** and **face-flux reconstruction**
are the measurable functions
$$ \mathcal U_m(x,t)=U_j^{m,n},\qquad \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} $$ whenever $(x,t)\in I_j^m\times J_n^m$. Values on cell or time-grid boundaries may be assigned arbitrarily, since those boundaries have two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. In particular, for almost every $(x,t)$, $$ \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=F\!\left(\mathcal U_m(x,t),\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)\right). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

derivations.claim: Fix a closed bounded interval $I$ and $T'<T$, with common state bound $M$ on $I\times[0,T']$. For $0<\epsilon<T'$, let $K=I\times[\epsilon,T']$. If $E=\{(x,t)\in K:|u(x,t)|>M\}$ had positive measure, then $E=\bigcup_{r\ge1}E_r$, where $E_r=\{(x,t)\in K:|u(x,t)|\ge M+1/r\}$. By countable subadditivity in [F3], some $E_r$ has positive measure. Since $|\mathcal U_m|\le M$ almost everywhere on $K$, it follows that $\|\mathcal U_m-u\|_{L^1(K)}\ge r^{-1}|E_r|>0$ for every $m$, contradicting strong $L^1$ convergence on $K$. Thus $|u|\le M$ almost everywhere on $K$. Taking $\epsilon=1/r$ for sufficiently large integers $r$ covers $I\times(0,T')$; any bounded interval is contained in a closed bounded one, so $u$ is locally essentially bounded up to $t=0$.

Fix $0<\epsilon<T'$ and a compact rectangle $K\subset\mathbb R\times[\epsilon,T']$. Enlarge its spatial interval by $1$; step 1.1 bounds $u$ there. The cutoff $v=u$ on this enlarged bounded rectangle and $v=0$ elsewhere is bounded and measurable, so [F3] makes $v\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$. For all large $m$, $h_m<1$. By [F2], $\|u(\cdot+h_m,\cdot)-u\|_{L^1(K)}\to0$: the cutoff agrees with $u$ on $K$ and on $K+h_m$. Also $K+h_m$ is contained in one fixed compact enlargement $K'$ for all large $m$, so strong local convergence gives $\|\mathcal U_m(\cdot+h_m,\cdot)-u(\cdot+h_m,\cdot)\|_{L^1(K)}=\|\mathcal U_m-u\|_{L^1(K+h_m)}\le\|\mathcal U_m-u\|_{L^1(K')}\to0$. The triangle inequality gives $\mathcal U_m(\cdot+h_m,\cdot)\to u$ in $L^1(K)$.

Let $K$ be as in step 2.1, and choose a common bound $M$ on the enlarged rectangle. The square $S=[-M,M]^2$ is a nonempty closed box, hence compact by [F4]. Continuity of $F$ and [F5] bound $F$ on $S$; [F6] makes it uniformly continuous there. Put $a_m=\mathcal U_m(x,t)$ and $b_m=\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)$. Steps 1.1–2.1 show both converge to $u$ in measure on $K$, and all three values lie in $[-M,M]$ almost everywhere. For $\delta>0$, the set where either input error is at least $\delta$ has measure at most $\delta^{-1}$ times the sum of the two $L^1$ errors. Uniform continuity makes $|F(a_m,b_m)-F(u,u)|$ arbitrarily small off this set, while boundedness of $F$ controls it on the set. Thus $F(a_m,b_m)\to F(u,u)=f(u)$ in $L^1(K)$. By [F1], $\mathcal Q_m\to f(u)$ in $L^1(K)$.

On $I\times(0,\epsilon)$, the local state bound on the interval enlarged by $1$ bounds both flux inputs, while step 1.1 bounds $u$. Continuity of $F$ and $f$ bounds $\mathcal Q_m$ and $f(u)$ there by one constant independent of $m$. Hence the integral of $|\mathcal Q_m-f(u)|$ over this strip is at most a constant times $|I|\epsilon$. Step 3.1 gives convergence on $I\times[\epsilon,T']$. Letting first $m\to\infty$ and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves convergence on $I\times(0,T']$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the cells, time levels, states and interface fluxes from
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. For $J_n^m=[t_n^m,t_{n+1}^m)$,
the **piecewise-constant state reconstruction** and **face-flux reconstruction**
are the measurable functions
$$ \mathcal U_m(x,t)=U_j^{m,n},\qquad \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} $$ whenever $(x,t)\in I_j^m\times J_n^m$. Values on cell or time-grid boundaries may be assigned arbitrarily, since those boundaries have two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. In particular, for almost every $(x,t)$, $$ \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=F\!\left(\mathcal U_m(x,t),\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)\right). $$

Let $(U_j^{m,n})$ be a scheme from
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]], with reconstruction
$(\mathcal U_m,\mathcal Q_m)$ as in
[[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]]. For a test function
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$, define its space-time
cell average
$$ \Phi_j^{m,n}=\frac1{h_m\tau_m}\int_{t_n^m}^{t_{n+1}^m}\int_{I_j^m}\varphi(x,t)\,dx\,dt. $$ If $N\ge1$ is such that $\varphi$ vanishes for $t\ge t_{N-1}^m$, then $$ \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}h_m U_j^{m,0}\Phi_j^{m,0} +\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}h_m U_j^{m,n} (\Phi_j^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n-1}) +\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\tau_m Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} (\Phi_{j+1}^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n})=0. $$
All sums are finite because $\varphi$ is compactly supported in space and time.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(\mathcal U_m,
\mathcal Q_m)$ be reconstructions from
[[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]] for schemes using a continuous
consistent flux $F$ for a continuous physical flux $f$ as in
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Suppose $h_m\to0$,
$\mathcal U_m\to u$ strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$, and
for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and $T'<T$ there is
$M_{I,T'}<\infty$ such that $|\mathcal U_m|\le M_{I,T'}$ almost everywhere on
$I\times[0,T']$ for every $m$. Then $u$ is locally essentially bounded up to
the initial face and, for every bounded interval $I$ and $T'<T$,
$$ \|\mathcal Q_m-f(u)\|_{L^1(I\times(0,T'))}\longrightarrow0. $$

Let $T>0$, let $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$. A measurable
function $u\colon\mathbb R\times(0,T)\to\mathbb R$ is a **locally bounded
distributional weak solution** of $u_t+f(u)_x=0$ with initial datum $u_0$ if
for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and every $T'<T$ it is
essentially bounded on $I\times(0,T')$, and, for every
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$ \int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0. $$
The integrals are local: if a test is supported in $I\times[-S,T']$ with $I$
bounded and $T'<T$, the local essential bound makes $u$ bounded on
$I\times(0,T']$, and continuity of $f$ makes $f(u)$ bounded on that bounded
range. The initial integral is finite because $u_0$ is locally integrable and
$\varphi(\cdot,0)$ is compactly supported. This is the local
integrability version of the weak identity in
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]], whose
published formulation assumes a global $L^\infty$ bound. This definition adds
no entropy inequality or strong local $L^1$ trace requirement.

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, let
$f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and let
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. A bounded
measurable $u\colon\Pi_T\to\mathbb R$ is a **distributional weak solution** of
the Cauchy problem $u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$, if for
every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n\times(-\infty,T))$ --- test functions
whose support may meet the initial plane $t=0$ --- one has
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\Bigl(u\,\varphi_t+f(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\Bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.$$
Equivalently $u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$, together
with the displayed initial boundary term
([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). The integrals are absolutely
convergent: $u$ is bounded, $f(u)$ is bounded on the bounded range of $u$, and
$\varphi$ has compact support, so the pairings are $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ pairings
and are representative-independent ([[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]; the product-space identities
are those of [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and
[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]). The condition is an
equality in the $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ classes of $u$ and $f(u)$; it involves no
pointwise assignment of $u$ on $\{t=0\}$, and the initial datum enters only
through the boundary term ([[def-scalar-conservation-law-and-flux]]). For the
entropy formulation of this page the initial condition is instead imposed as a
strong local $L^1$ trace ([[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]).

derivations.claim: Fix $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$. Its time support on $[0,T)$ is contained in $[0,T_\varphi]$ for some $T_\varphi<T$. For all sufficiently large $m$, choose $N_m\ge3$ with $T_\varphi<t_{N_m-2}^m<t_{N_m-1}^m<t_{N_m}^m<T$. By [F1] and [F2] these are precisely the scheme states and face fluxes of the reconstruction, so [F3] gives the exact summed update identity for this test.

The initial term in [F3] converges to the desired boundary term. Indeed, $h_mU_j^{m,0}=\int_{I_j^m}u_0$, while $\Phi_j^{m,0}$ is the average of $\varphi$ on $I_j^m\times[0,\tau_m)$. Smoothness gives $|\Phi_j^{m,0}-\varphi(x,0)|\le C_\varphi(h_m+\tau_m)$ for $x\in I_j^m$; summing the resulting errors over the finitely many cells meeting the support bounds the total by $C_\varphi(h_m+\tau_m)\int_K|u_0|\to0$ on a fixed compact $K$.

For $n\ge1$, the difference $\Phi_j^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n-1}$ differs from $h_m^{-1}\int_{I_j^m}\int_{J_n^m}\varphi_t$ by at most $C_\varphi\tau_m^2$, by Taylor's formula in time for the smooth function $t\mapsto h_m^{-1}\int_{I_j^m}\varphi(x,t)\,dx$. After multiplication by $h_mU_j^{m,n}$ and summation over $O(h_m^{-1})$ cells and $O(\tau_m^{-1})$ time slabs in the fixed support, the total error is $O(\tau_m)$. The missing first-slab integral is also $O(\tau_m)$ because $|\mathcal U_m|$ is uniformly bounded on the compact support and $\varphi_t$ is bounded. Hence the time sum in [F3] differs from $\int_0^T\int\mathcal U_m\varphi_t$ by a quantity tending to zero.

For each $j,n$, translation of a cell interval and the fundamental theorem of calculus give $\tau_m(\Phi_{j+1}^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n}) =\int_{J_n^m}\int_{I_j^m}\frac1{h_m}\int_0^{h_m}\varphi_x(x+s,t)\,ds\,dx\,dt$. Its difference from $\int_{J_n^m}\int_{I_j^m}\varphi_x$ is at most $C_\varphi h_m^2\tau_m$, by the bound on $\varphi_{xx}$. The numerical face fluxes are uniformly bounded on cells meeting the test support because $F$ is continuous on the compact state square supplied by local boundedness. Summing over the finitely many cells and time slabs meeting the test support gives total error $O(h_m)$. Thus the flux sum in [F3] differs from $\int_0^T\int\mathcal Q_m\varphi_x$ by a quantity tending to zero.

Strong local $L^1$ convergence gives $\int\mathcal U_m\varphi_t\to\int u\varphi_t$ on times bounded away from zero. On $I\times(0,\epsilon)$, the local uniform bound for both $\mathcal U_m$ and $u$ makes the integral difference at most a constant times $|I|\epsilon$; letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves convergence on the full test support. By [F4], $\int\mathcal Q_m\varphi_x\to\int f(u)\varphi_x$ on that support. Step 2.1 gives the initial term limit, and steps 2.2–2.3 identify the limits of the discrete sums. Taking the limit in [F3] proves the weak identity. By [F4], $u$ is locally essentially bounded, and [F5] identifies it as the stated local weak solution.

the **piecewise-constant state reconstruction** and **face-flux reconstruction**
are the measurable functions
$$ \mathcal U_m(x,t)=U_j^{m,n},\qquad \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} $$ whenever $(x,t)\in I_j^m\times J_n^m$. In particular, for almost every $(x,t)$, $$ \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=F\!\left(\mathcal U_m(x,t),\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)\right). $$

For Burgers' flux $f_B(s)=s^2/2$, define $G\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ as follows. If $a\le b$, set
$$ G(a,b)=\begin{cases} a^2/2,&a\ge0,\\ b^2/2,&a<0\text{ and }b\le0,\\ 0,&a<0<b. \end{cases} $$ If $b<a$, set $$ G(a,b)=\frac12\max\{a^2,b^2\}. $$
This is the Godunov flux for the convex Burgers flux: for increasing states it
uses the minimum of $f_B$ on $[a,b]$, and for decreasing states it uses the
maximum of $f_B$ on $[b,a]$. It is proposed as a particular numerical flux in
the scheme of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Its continuity and
consistency are verified in the pair.

The map $G$ defined in [[def-godunov-flux-for-burgers]] is continuous on

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $T>0$, $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, $u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$, and $F\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $F(a,a)=f(a)$ for every $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $m$, form the conservative finite-volume scheme and space-time reconstruction of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]] and [[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]] using $h_m,\tau_m\to0$ and initial cell averages of $u_0$. Suppose reconstructions converge strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$ to $u$, and for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and $T'<T$ there is $M_{I,T'}<\infty$ such that $|\mathcal U_m|\le M_{I,T'}$ almost everywhere on $I\times[0,T']$ for every $m$. Then $u$ is a locally bounded distributional weak solution in the sense of [[def-locally-bounded-distributional-weak-solution]]; explicitly, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$
\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.
$$
The strong convergence and local uniform bounds are hypotheses, not conclusions. No CFL condition or entropy inequality is assumed, so the theorem proves a weak limit only; it does not claim Kruzhkov entropy admissibility. If the limit is also globally essentially bounded, this identity is the published bounded weak formulation in [[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]].

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$
([[def-scalar-conservation-law-and-flux]]), and let $u$ be a piecewise $C^1$
distributional weak solution
([[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]]) with
two-sided $C^1$ interface $\Gamma$ and traces as in
[[def-piecewise-smooth-shock-and-one-sided-traces]]. Orient the unit
space--time normal $\nu=(\nu_t,\nu_x)$ from the minus side to the plus side.
Then at every $\zeta\in\Gamma\subset U$,
$$[u](\zeta)\nu_t(\zeta)+[f](\zeta)\cdot\nu_x(\zeta)=0,$$
where $[u]=u^+-u^-$ and $[f]=f(u^+)-f(u^-)$.

In one space dimension, for a graph $x=s(t)$ with minus side $x<s(t)$ and plus
side $x>s(t)$, $\nu=(-s'(t),1)/\sqrt{1+s'(t)^2}$, so the condition is
$s'(t)[u](t)=[f](t)$ at every graph point. If $[u]\ne0$ in one dimension, then
$s'=[f]/[u]$; if $[u]=0$, then $[f]=0$ and the relation is $0=0$, with no speed
constraint.

derivations.claim: The cell averages are $1$ for $j<0$ and $-1$ for $j\ge0$. The only face pairs are $(1,1)$, $(1,-1)$, and $(-1,-1)$; [F3] gives flux $1/2$ in all three cases.

Every cell therefore has equal left and right fluxes at every step, so the update leaves every $U_j^{m,n}$ unchanged. Induction on $n$ gives exactly the stationary step profile displayed in the Example.
The reconstruction equals that stationary profile almost everywhere for all $m$, so it converges strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and is bounded by $1$. The weak-limit theorem [F4] applies.
The traces are $u^-=1$ and $u^+=-1$. Thus [F5] gives $s=(f_B(-1)-f_B(1))/(-1-1)=(1/2-1/2)/(-2)=0$, agreeing with the stationary interface.

derivations.claim: Use the compact rectangle $K=[0,1]\times[1/4,3/4]$ inside the space-time domain. Each $V_k$ takes only the values $-1,1$ on $[0,1)\times(0,1)$ and zero outside, so $|V_k|\le1$ and $\|V_k\|_{L^1(K)}=1/2$.

If $k<\ell$, every $k$-cell in $[0,1)$ is the union of $2^{\ell-k}$ finer $\ell$-cells, an even number. The signs of $V_\ell$ alternate on those finer cells, so their integral on each coarse cell is zero; since $V_k$ is constant on that coarse cell, $\int_KV_kV_\ell=0$.

For signs $a,b\in\{-1,1\}$, $|a-b|=1-ab$. Thus for $k\ne\ell$, $$ \|V_k-V_\ell\|_{L^1(K)} =1/2-\int_KV_kV_\ell=1/2. $$ Every subsequence is therefore non-Cauchy in $L^1(K)$, so no subsequence can converge strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
This example supplies only a bounded sequence without strong compactness; it makes no finite-volume recurrence claim. Therefore the convergence premise in [F1] remains a separate hypothesis.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the cells, time levels, states and interface fluxes from

are the measurable functions
$$ \mathcal U_m(x,t)=U_j^{m,n},\qquad \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=Q_{j+1/2}^{m,n} $$ whenever $(x,t)\in I_j^m\times J_n^m$. In particular, for almost every $(x,t)$, $$ \mathcal Q_m(x,t)=F\!\left(\mathcal U_m(x,t),\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)\right). $$

Suppose reconstructions converge strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$ to $u$, and for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and $T'<T$ there is $M_{I,T'}<\infty$ such that $|\mathcal U_m|\le M_{I,T'}$ almost everywhere on $I\times[0,T']$ for every $m$. Then $u$ is a locally bounded distributional weak solution in the sense of [[def-locally-bounded-distributional-weak-solution]]; explicitly, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$
\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.
$$

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$, and
$\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$. The unknown and initial datum are equivalence
classes $[u]\in L^\infty(\Pi_T)$ and
$[u_0]\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, where
equality is Lebesgue-a.e. ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]).

For $k\in\mathbb R$ define the **Kruzhkov entropy pair**
$$\eta_k(s)=|s-k|,\qquad q_k(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)\bigl(f(s)-f(k)\bigr),$$
with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then $\eta_k$ is convex
and $q_k'=\eta_k'f'$ almost everywhere, so $(\eta_k,q_k)$ is a locally Lipschitz convex
entropy--entropy flux pair ([[def-convex-entropy-entropy-flux-pair]]).

The class $[u]$ is a **Kruzhkov entropy solution** of
$u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ with initial trace $[u_0]$ if:

(i) for every $k\in\mathbb R$ and every nonnegative
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Pi_T)$,
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\bigl(\eta_k(u)\,\varphi_t+q_k(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\bigr)\,dx\,dt\ge0,$$
that is, $\partial_t\eta_k(u)+\operatorname{div}_x q_k(u)\le0$ in
$\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$; and

(ii) for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{0<t<\min\{\delta,T\}}\int_K|u(t,x)-u_0(x)|\,dx=0.$$

The integral in (i) is independent of the representative because its integrand
is unchanged almost everywhere. For (ii), Fubini's theorem gives locally
integrable spatial sections for almost every $t$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the
displayed slice integral is defined for those times and its essential supremum
ignores the exceptional null set. If $u$ or $u_0$ is changed on a null set in
its respective space, Fubini's theorem shows that the slice-integral function
changes only for a null set of times, so the trace condition is well defined on
the equivalence classes: this is the **strong local $L^1$ initial trace**.

Taking $k$ above and below the essential range of $u$ makes $\eta_k$ equal
$k-u$ and $u-k$, whose $t$- and $x$-derivatives cancel the constant terms
against compactly supported test functions, so the entropy inequalities imply
the weak conservation law of
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]] tested
against nonnegative test functions, hence by linearity against all test
functions.

To recover the Cauchy boundary term, apply the interior weak identity to
$\varphi(t,x)\zeta(t/\delta)$, where $\zeta$ is smooth and nondecreasing,
$\zeta=0$ on $(-\infty,1/2]$ and $\zeta=1$ on $[1,\infty)$.
For $\delta>0$ this product is supported away from $t=0$, so it is
an admissible interior test. The term containing $\zeta'/\delta$
converges to $\int u_0(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx$ by (ii), while the other terms
converge on the compact support. This proves the full weak formulation with
initial datum $u_0$, rather than only its interior equation.

derivations.claim: Cell averages of $u_0$ are $U_j^{m,0}=0$ for $j<0$ and $1$ for $j\ge0$. The only face pairs along the resulting step are $(0,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$; [F3] gives their fluxes as $0,0,1/2$. The ratio $\tau_m/h_m=2$, while $\max_{0\le s\le1}|f'_B(s)|=1$, so the usual noninteraction bound $(\tau_m/h_m)\max|f'_B|\le1$ fails.

Assume inductively $U_j^{m,n}=0$ for $j<n$ and $1$ for $j\ge n$. If $j<n$, both face fluxes are $0$, so the state remains $0$. At $j=n$, the left flux is $0$ and the right flux is $1/2$, hence $U_n^{m,n+1}=1-2(1/2-0)=0$. For $j>n$ both fluxes are $1/2$, so those states remain $1$. Therefore the step shifts to $U_j^{m,n+1}=0$ for $j<n+1$ and $1$ for $j\ge n+1$.

On $[2nh_m,2(n+1)h_m)$, the numerical jump is at $nh_m$, while the limit jump is at $t/2\in[nh_m,(n+1)h_m)$. The profiles differ only on a strip of width at most $h_m$ and height $1$, so the $L^1$ error on every bounded space-time rectangle is at most $h_mT'\to0$. All states are bounded by $1$. By [F4], the limit $u(x,t)=0$ for $x<t/2$ and $1$ for $x>t/2$ is a locally bounded distributional weak solution with those initial data.

Take $k=1/2$. Then $\eta_k(0)=\eta_k(1)=1/2$, while $q_k(0)=1/8$ and $q_k(1)=3/8$. Choose nonnegative $\alpha\in C_c^\infty((0,T))$ with $\int\alpha>0$ and nonnegative $\beta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\beta(0)>0$, and set $\psi(x,t)=\alpha(t)\beta(x-t/2)$. This is an admissible nonnegative test. To evaluate its time term, put $B=\int_{\mathbb R}\beta(y)\,dy$. Differentiating the smooth compactly supported test and changing variables gives $\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_t(x,t)\,dx=B\alpha'(t)-\frac12\alpha(t)\int_{\mathbb R}\beta'(y)\,dy=B\alpha'(t)$; the last integral is zero because $\beta$ is compactly supported. Therefore $\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\eta_k(u)\psi_t\,dx\,dt=\frac12B(\alpha(T)-\alpha(0))=0$. Splitting the flux integral at $x=t/2$ and applying the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\int_{\mathbb R}q_k(u)\psi_x\,dx=(1/8-3/8)\psi(t/2,t)=-\frac14\alpha(t)\beta(0)$. Thus the integral in [F5] equals $-\frac14\beta(0)\int\alpha<0$, contradicting the required entropy inequality. The weak limit is not Kruzhkov entropic.
